title: Winter and Hymn
premise: Quentin Halloran, a hospice nurse haunted by the backwards counting of the dying, discovers that every photograph from his late grandmother's house now contains an extra chair — and that the chair moves closer in each image. The chair belongs to Hymn, an entity his grandmother bargained with decades ago to save a life, a debt now due to be collected from the last living signer of the family's covenant papers. As Quentin documents the haunting in his clinical notebooks, he uncovers that his grandmother's mercy was also a theft: she stole a neighbor's identity to seal the bargain, and the wronged dead have been counting backwards ever since. To survive until sunrise, Quentin must choose between destroying the papers and letting the debt pass to an innocent hospice resident, ultimately signing the covenant himself and surrendering his own name to Hymn — becoming, in the final photographs, the one seated in the chair.
about_author: I. M. Halloran is the pseudonymous pen of a former palliative care worker who spent eleven years recording the final words of the dying in a series of sealed notebooks. Winter and Hymn is their second novel, written entirely between the hours of midnight and dawn.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Night shift at Rosewood Hospice: Mrs. Abernathy counts down from one hundred, and every dying patient does the same, always reaching zero at the exact moment of death. Quentin documents it in his notebook, treating the ritual as clinical data and private prayer. Emotional beat: the eerie calm of a man who has made a religion of observation.

chapters.title: Inventory of Rooms
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Clearing his grandmother's house after her funeral, Quentin photographs every room for the estate inventory. Only later, reviewing the images, does he notice a plain wooden chair in the corner of the parlor — a chair that was never there. Beat: the first crack in his rational worldview.

chapters.title: The Chair Moves
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Comparing old family albums with new photos, Quentin realizes the chair appears in photographs going back decades, always slightly closer to the camera, closer to the people. His sister Dee insists he's grieving. Beat: dread sharpening into obsession.

chapters.title: Papers in the Floor
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Beneath a loose floorboard he finds a leather folio: a covenant, signed 1968 by his grandmother, written in a hand that isn't hers, promising 'one seat at the winter table.' A neighbor's name is crossed out violently. Beat: the discovery that mercy had a price.

chapters.title: Hymn
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. At the hospice, a new admission with no records introduces himself only as Hymn, and the other patients begin counting backwards in unison when he passes. Quentin's documentation becomes frantic, less like prayer than evidence-gathering. Beat: the watcher realizes he is watched.

chapters.title: What Dee Remembers
chapters.summary: POV Dee. Quentin's sister recalls being five, watching Grandma speak to an empty chair at Christmas, thanking it. She remembers a neighbor boy, Tomas Voss, who 'went away' in 1968 and was never spoken of again. Beat: grief and complicity entwined.

chapters.title: The Voss File
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. At the county archive, Quentin learns Tomas Voss didn't leave — his identity was absorbed, his records rewritten into his grandmother's history. The covenant's signature is Tomas's, forged. Beat: justice outside the law becomes personal.

chapters.title: Zero
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Mrs. Abernathy reaches zero at 3:11 a.m., and in the death-room photograph Quentin takes out of habit, the chair is there, occupied, facing the camera. Hymn signs himself in as her replacement resident. Beat: documentation can no longer protect him.

chapters.title: Invitation
chapters.summary: POV Hymn. For the first time, the entity's voice: courteous, patient, endlessly reasonable. Hymn explains the covenant is a seat at a winter table, and a table needs guests; the debt falls to the last signer's blood. He compliments Quentin's notebooks. Beat: seduction of the meticulous mind.

chapters.title: Burning the Folio
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Quentin burns the covenant in his sink; the ash reassembles in the folio by morning, now bearing a fresh line: 'Quentin Halloran, pending.' Dee begs him to walk away from the house entirely. Beat: denial collapsing into terror.

chapters.title: The Neighbor's Grave
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. At the pauper's cemetery Quentin finds Tomas Voss's grave, unmarked except for a wooden chair someone has placed on it. The backwards counting, he realizes, is Tomas — still counting down the life that was stolen from him. Beat: sympathy for the haunting.

chapters.title: Winter Table
chapters.summary: POV Dee. Dee dreams of the parlor set for a feast, six chairs, seven place settings. She wakes to find frost on the inside of her windows and her own handwriting on the dream: 'bring him home.' Beat: the haunting reaches past Quentin to the bloodline.

chapters.title: The Last Resident
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. The hospice's final signer of anything — elderly Mr. Aldous, dying, lucid — reveals he witnessed the 1968 bargain as a boy and has been counting backwards his whole life, waiting to reach zero. He offers to sign the covenant over to himself, a stranger's mercy repaying a stranger's theft. Beat: grace offered at the eleventh hour.

chapters.title: Terms of Surrender
chapters.summary: POV Hymn. Hymn explains why he cannot simply take: the covenant binds the collector as much as the collected, and a seat freely offered is the only meal he may accept. He shows Quentin the winter table in full — the guests are all the identities the family consumed. Beat: horror reframed as terrible fairness.

chapters.title: Aldous at Zero
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Aldous signs, begins counting, and reaches zero at dawn — but the chair in the photographs doesn't empty. Hymn appears at the hospice desk, apologetic: a signature given in mercy is not a signature given in debt. The seat remains Quentin's. Beat: the collapse of the escape route.

chapters.title: Everything Documented
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Quentin reads his own notebooks cover to cover and finds entries in his handwriting he never wrote, dated for the next six nights, each ending with the word 'seated.' Beat: identity dissolving; memory no longer trustworthy.

chapters.title: Tomas Speaks
chapters.summary: POV Tomas. The stolen boy's voice, counting at last toward something instead of down from something: he doesn't want Quentin's soul — he wants his name back, spoken aloud, witnessed, restored. Beat: the true debt is not payment but recognition.

chapters.title: The Longest Night
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Winter solstice. Quentin seals himself in the grandmother's parlor until sunrise, covenant on the table, notebook in hand, chair across from him slowly filling. He drafts three documents: a confession of his grandmother's theft, a restoration of Tomas's name, and a blank line for his own. Beat: held breath.

chapters.title: Signature
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. As the chair becomes occupied and the frost writes words on the windows, Quentin signs — not the covenant, but the confession, naming Tomas Voss aloud and giving him back his history. Hymn rises, hungry, insisting a seat was still offered. Beat: the climax's hinge — truth given, debt still claimed.

chapters.title: Seated
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. To satisfy the letter of the bargain, Quentin sits in the chair himself until sunrise, offering his presence, not his name — a nurse keeping vigil, the one act his whole life has trained him for. The counting outside the windows reaches zero as the sun crests. Beat: sacrifice as vocation.

chapters.title: The Empty Chair
chapters.summary: POV Dee. Dee arrives at dawn to find the parlor warm, the covenant ash, the chair empty, and Quentin asleep in his own notebook's final entry — in his own handwriting at last. In every photograph in the house, the extra chair is gone. Beat: release, and the ache of what it cost.

chapters.title: Vigil
chapters.summary: POV Quentin, epilogue. Back on the hospice night shift, Quentin no longer fears the counting; he counts along now, softly, and when a dying woman reaches zero she smiles at the empty corner of the room. His new notebook's first page reads only a name: Tomas Voss, restored. Beat: justice witnessed, identity kept, memory made into prayer.
